## TL;DR

This round fixed both review findings without loosening the fail-closed policy: inspection errors can no longer masquerade as proof that data is disposable, and the generated-path allowlist is now scoped to known build locations instead of matching any directory named `dist`, `coverage`, or `.repoos`. While tracing the same class I found a third fail-open instance — `existsSync` collapsing a permission error into "directory vanished" — and fixed it too. I also removed the stale round-report JSONs the reviewer flagged and updated the worktree-GC documentation. The worktree-GC suite passes with new regression tests for symlink loops, unreadable git blobs, nested look-alike build directories, and tracked dirty files under `dist`.

## Work and rationale

The first finding was a fail-open class. `isSymlinkInto` became `ignoredPathIsProvablyRedundant`: only `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` count as a confirmed absence; `ELOOP`, `EACCES`, `EIO`, and any other error now retain the worktree. `gitRunBytes` collapsed every `git show` failure to `null`, so a permission or timeout error looked exactly like a deleted task file. It is replaced by `gitBlobAt`, which uses `ls-tree` to establish whether the path exists in the revision (exit 0 with empty output for a confirmed absence), then `cat-file` for the bytes. The result is a tagged `present` / `absent` / `unreadable` value; only `absent` means deletion. Every unreadable result is threaded through a new `Representation.inspectionError` so the retention reason is actionable (`could not inspect branch content: ...`) rather than a generic "commits not represented".

I then traced the same error-conflation pattern through every filesystem presence check. `existsSync` was used to decide a worktree directory had vanished, but it returns `false` for `EACCES`/`EIO` as well as `ENOENT`; a permission failure could therefore look like a vanished directory. A small `pathPresence` helper now returns `present` / `missing` / `unknown`, and every caller retains on `unknown` (including the dirty-task-file read and both vanished-directory branches).

The second finding was the unscoped allowlist. `dist`, `coverage`, and `.repoos` are now recognized only at the repository root (plus the docs site's `.vitepress` build/cache), and the root cache directory comes from the live config. A nested `src/tool/dist`, `src/tool/coverage`, or `src/tool/.repoos` is treated as possible local data. I also removed the separate `isGeneratedBuildPath` filter from the dirty-path loop: a tracked dirty file is a real uncommitted change even when its path looks like build output, so it is never discarded by path alone. `node_modules` remains disposable at any depth because it is dependency output rather than tracked source.

## Approaches tried

For the unreadable-blob regression I needed a deterministic inspection error. I made the test repository keep objects loose (`gc.auto=0`), resolved the blob's SHA, and `chmod 000`'d that single loose object. `git status`, `git diff --name-only`, and `ls-tree` still succeed; `cat-file` fails with EACCES. It is skipped as root. For the symlink case I used a self-referential `.env` link: `lstat` succeeds, `realpath` throws ELOOP. The other cases are table-driven.

## Challenges and blockers

The main trap was that the sweep extracted only `differing` and `uniqueTaskFiles` from the proof, silently dropping `inspectionError`, which made the new test fail with the old generic reason. Collecting the error into the final reason fixed it. The nested-path tests also had to account for `git status --ignored=matching` collapsing ignored directories to a single `dir/` entry.

## Key learnings

Fail-closed cleanup needs an explicit three-way "present / absent / unknown" result at every inspection boundary; a nullable return type invites conflating absence with failure. Likewise, "looks like a build directory" is not proof of generated output — scope fabricated paths to known roots rather than matching segments, and never let a path-shape rule suppress tracked uncommitted work.
